Glossary

    Number and operations

    Words: 1864

    From natural numbers to real ones: each extension of number appeared in order to carry out an operation that could not be carried out before. The laws of operations did not change along the way.

    Main idea of the page #

    Subtraction gave rise to negative numbers, division to fractions, taking roots to irrational numbers. But the commutative, associative and distributive laws that worked for counting objects work for all real numbers too. This block is the foundation: the rest of algebra is these laws written with letters. It can count and compare exactly; it does not say how two quantities depend on each other - that is already a function (block 5).

    Step 0 · Hook

    1 · Minus two squared #

    What is −22-2^2? The usual answer: «minus times minus is plus, so 4». But in the notation −22-2^2 only the two is squared, and the minus stands in front of the result: −22=−(22)=−4-2^2 = -(2^2) = -4. To square −2 itself you need brackets: (−2)2=4(-2)^2 = 4.

    The second hook: |−5+2||-5 + 2|. The habit «absolute value removes the minuses» gives 5+2=75 + 2 = 7. In fact the operation inside is done first: |−3|=3|-3| = 3. Neither mistake comes from not knowing the rules; both come from reading the notation «by eye».

    Step 1 · Concept

    2 · How number grew #

    • Natural numbers ℕ\mathbb{N}: 1, 2, 3, … - the numbers of counting. You can always add and multiply, but not always subtract.
    • Integers ℤ\mathbb{Z}: zero and the negative numbers are added. Now subtraction is always possible, but division is not.
    • Rational numberA number that can be written as a fraction p/q with an integer p and a natural q.To the glossary ℚ\mathbb{Q}: fractions pq\frac{p}{q}, where p is an integer and q is natural. Division by any number except zero is possible. Every rational fraction is a terminating or a recurring decimal.
    • Real numbersAll rational and irrational numbers together: every point of the number line.To the glossary ℝ\mathbb{R}: Irrational numberA real number that cannot be written as a common fraction.To the glossary are added - infinite non-recurring decimals, like 2\sqrt{2} or π. Now every point of the number line has its number.

    Figure 1. Each set of numbers lies inside the next one, and each extension came for the sake of a new operation.

    The Absolute valueThe distance from a number to zero on the number line; an absolute value is never negative.To the glossary of a number is its distance to zero on the number line, so an absolute value is never negative. An IntervalAll the numbers between two bounds; a square bracket includes the bound, a round one does not.To the glossary is the set of all numbers between two bounds: a square bracket means the bound is included, a round one means it is not.

    Figure 2. Absolute value is the distance to zero: |−3| = |3| = 3.

    Step 2 · Law

    3 · Laws of operations #

    Distributive law

    a(b+c)=ab+aca(b + c) = ab + ac

    Together with the commutative ab=baab = ba and associative (ab)c=a(bc)(ab)c = a(bc) laws it holds up all of algebra.

    Zero product

    ab=0⟺a=0 or b=0ab = 0 \iff a = 0 \text{ or } b = 0

    Absolute value is distance to zero

    |a|={a,a≥0−a,a<0|a| = \begin{cases} a, & a \geq 0 \\ -a, & a < 0 \end{cases}

    And two corollaries: |ab|=|a|·|b||ab| = |a| \cdot |b|, |a+b|≤|a|+|b||a + b| \leq |a| + |b|.

    Tests for divisibility by 3 and by 9

    A number is divisible by 3 (by 9) if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 (by 9). For 2, 5 and 10 you look at the last digit.

    The product of the GCD and the LCM equals the product of the numbers

    GCD(a,b)·LCM(a,b)=a·b\text{GCD}(a, b) \cdot \text{LCM}(a, b) = a \cdot b
    Step 3 · Why it is so

    4 · Where these laws come from #

    The distributive law is the area of a rectangle with side a and a second side made of the segments b and c: it can be counted as a whole or in two pieces. All the Formulas of short multiplicationReady-made expansions of products, each of them a consequence of the distributive law.To the glossary stand on it (block 3).

    Figure 3. The distributive law as area: a(b + c) = ab + ac.

    Zero productA product equals zero if and only if at least one factor equals zero.To the glossary . Let ab=0ab = 0 and a≠0a \neq 0. Multiply both sides by 1a\frac{1}{a}: we get b=0b = 0. That is exactly why equations are solved by factorising: a product equals zero only when a factor equals zero.

    Divisibility testA rule that shows whether a number is divisible without doing the division.To the glossary for 9. 10=9+110 = 9 + 1, 100=99+1100 = 99 + 1, and so on for every place value. So

    3456=3·999+4·99+5·9+(3+4+5+6)3456 = 3 \cdot 999 + 4 \cdot 99 + 5 \cdot 9 + (3 + 4 + 5 + 6)

    The first three terms are always divisible by 9, so everything is decided by the sum of the digits. The same holds for 3, because 9 is divisible by 3.

    GCD and LCMThe greatest common divisor and the least common multiple of two natural numbers.To the glossary and LCM. The GCD takes each prime factor at the lower of its two powers, the LCM at the higher. Together they take each factor exactly as many times as it occurs in a and b together, that is, they give the product ab.

    Step 4 · Limits

    5 · Where the laws break #

    You do not divide by zero. This is not a teacher's ban but a consequence: if 50=x\frac{5}{0} = x, then x·0=5x \cdot 0 = 5, while any number multiplied by zero gives zero.

    |a+b|=|a|+|b||a + b| = |a| + |b| only when a and b have the same sign (or at least one of them is zero). For numbers of different signs the absolute value of the sum is smaller.

    The order of operations is a convention, not a law. A power is done before multiplication and before the minus sign in front of a number, multiplication before addition. So −22=−4-2^2 = -4, and only brackets can change the order.

    Tests by the last digit work only for 2, 5 and 10. For 4 you look at the last two digits, for 8 at the last three, and a number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible both by 2 and by 3.

    Step 5 · Practice

    6 · Tasks in the NMT format #

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Calculate −22+(−2)2-2^2 + (-2)^2.

    Law: order of operations.

    −4+4=0-4 + 4 = 0. The answer 8 comes from the blind move «both terms are 4».

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Which of the numbers is divisible by 9?

    Law: test for divisibility by 9.

    Digit sums: 10, 18, 26, 25, 10. Only 18 is divisible by 9. The number 9001 starts with a nine, but the test looks at the sum of all the digits.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Find the least common multiple of 12 and 18.

    Law: GCD and LCM.

    12=22·312 = 2^2 \cdot 3, 18=2·3218 = 2 \cdot 3^2. The LCM takes the highest powers: 22·32=362^2 \cdot 3^2 = 36. Check: GCD = 6, and 6·36=216=12·186 \cdot 36 = 216 = 12 \cdot 18.

    Matching · 3 points

    Match each expression (1-3) with its value (A-E).

    A · 4   B · 10   C · −4   D · 21   E · −10

    Law: absolute value and its limit for numbers of different signs.

    1) 7 + 3 = 10; 2) |−4| = 4: the absolute value of the sum is smaller than the sum of the absolute values, because the signs differ; 3) 3 − 7 = −4: a difference of absolute values can be negative, an absolute value cannot.

    Short answer · 2 points

    How many integers belong to the interval [−2.5; 3)[-2.5;\ 3)?

    Concept: interval.

    The integers −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. The bound 3 is not included (round bracket), −2.5 is not an integer. Answer: 5.
    Step 6 · Reverse move

    7 · Name the law yourself #

    The law is not given. Name it first, then calculate.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Calculate 37·54+37·4637 \cdot 54 + 37 \cdot 46.

    Law: the distributive law, read from right to left.

    37·(54+46)=37·100=370037 \cdot (54 + 46) = 37 \cdot 100 = 3700. The law works both ways: expanding brackets and taking out a common factor are one equality.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Solve the equation (x−3)(x+5)=0(x - 3)(x + 5) = 0. Write the sum of the roots as your answer.

    Law: zero product.

    A product equals zero when one of the factors is zero: x=3x = 3 or x=−5x = -5. Sum: −2. Expanding the brackets is unnecessary here: the law gives the roots at once.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Write the number 2.(3)2.(3) as a common fraction in lowest terms. Write its numerator as your answer.

    Concept: a rational number as a recurring decimal.

    Let x=2.333…x = 2.333\ldots. Then 10x=23.333…10x = 23.333\ldots, and the difference is 9x=219x = 21, x=73x = \frac{7}{3}. The recurring part disappears under subtraction, which is why every recurring decimal is rational.

    8 · Find the mistake in someone else's solution #

    Marko writes: «The equality |x|=−x|x| = -x is impossible, because an absolute value is always positive and −x-x is negative».

    Where is the mistake?

    The expression −x-x is not necessarily negative: for x=−4x = -4 it equals 4. By the definition of absolute value, |x|=−x|x| = -x exactly when x≤0x \leq 0. Marko confused «a minus in the notation» with «the sign of the number». One more detail: an absolute value is not «always positive» but non-negative - |0|=0|0| = 0.

    What you have after this page #

    Three laws of operations and absolute value as distance. Everything that will later be called «identity transformations» is the distributive, commutative and associative laws, and solving equations by factorising is the law of the zero product.

    Frequency on this site, not in the NMT: this page has 8 trainer tasks, and they lean on these laws: A rational number as a recurring decimal - 1, Absolute value is distance to zero - 1, Distributive law - 1, Interval - 1, Order of operations - 1, Tests for divisibility by 3 and by 9 - 1, The product of the GCD and the LCM equals the product of the numbers - 1, Zero product - 1. In real NMT papers of 2024-2026 this block is needed in 9 tasks out of 132: Absolute value is distance to zero - 6, How number grew - 2, Distributive law - 1.

    You know this block if you:

    1. solve 8 tasks out of 10 on the order of operations, absolute value and divisibility without a hint;
    2. can explain aloud why the test for divisibility by 9 looks at the sum of the digits;
    3. find the mistake in someone else's solution, as in Marko's.
